name: Bengaluru fort heritage walk
description: Discover the history of the Bengaluru fort on this walk. The Fort though today reduced to a mere fraction of its original expanse—less than 5%—remains one of the most significant remnants of the city’s pre-colonial past. This heritage walk invites you to step into the vestiges of a fort that once bore witness to battles transitions of power architectural ingenuity and political resilience.The fort began as a modest mud structure before being fortified with stone during Hyder Ali’s rule and later expanded under his son Tipu Sultan. These walls though weathered by time preserve within them the layered narratives of a growing urban center and the complexities of South Indian resistance to British expansion.A highlight of the walk is the iconic Tipu Sultan’s Summer Palace a rare example of Indo-Islamic architecture with its intricate wooden pillars frescoes and elegant symmetry. Once the seat of royal administration and leisure the palace offers insights not only into architectural aesthetics but also into the socio-political life of the Sultanate in the 18th century.As we navigate the narrow lanes of Old Bengaluru one encounters a little-known but historically important site: a surviving armoury tucked into the urban sprawl and forgotten by modern maps. Used during Tipu’s reign this structure is a physical testament to the city’s martial past and the strategic importance of Bangalore in Mysore’s military planning.A focal point of this walk is the Battle of Bangalore (1791) a critical campaign during the Third Anglo-Mysore War. The battle pitted the British East India Company against Tipu Sultan’s forces and highlighted not only the military prowess of the Sultanate but also broader geopolitical shifts—especially the fallout of British actions in other global theatres such as in the American Revolutionary War.It is particularly notable that the Mysorean rockets used innovatively during this time caught the attention of British military observers. Some of these designs later found their way into documentation that would influence the development of European—and even American—military technology. Legend holds that they partly inspired Francis Scott Key’s reference to "the rockets' red glare" in the Star-Spangled Banner.Finally the walk concludes with a return to the present—by way of South Indian culinary tradition offering participants a curated local snack and a cup of filter coffee. A reminder that history does not only reside in books or ruins—it lives on in tastes traditions and memories.This walking tour is not just about stones and structures. It is a curated window into Bengaluru’s transformation—from fortified stronghold and seat of regional power to colonial outpost and finally to modern metropolis. In walking its paths we do not merely observe history; we retrace it.Note : "This walk is led by a Bengaluru native and professional architect who has lived and studied in the vicinity of the fort for over three decades. His deep-rooted connection to the area combined with his architectural expertise gives him an intimate knowledge of not just every corner of the fort but also the rich history that surrounds it."

name: Johnson market heritage walk.
description: Most visitors pass through Johnson Market seeing only a bustling bazaar. Yet behind its lively streets lies one of Bengaluru's most fascinating and least explored historical quarters, where the stories of Britain, Persia, Arabia and South India have intertwined for nearly two centuries.This carefully curated walk takes you through these forgotten crossroads, where British colonial planning met ancient trade routes, and where merchants, Arabian horse traders and pilgrims from distant lands helped shape the city.Discover why the market bears the name of a British administrator, yet evolved into a thriving commercial district enriched by Persian and Arab influences. Follow the legacy of Aga Ali Asker, whose Arabian horse trade left an enduring mark on the princely State of Mysore.Explore the traditions of Bengaluru's Shia community through stories of Karbala, visit serene Sufi shrines and historic churches, and discover how diverse communities lived and flourished side by side.Interwoven with these histories are the flavours that have made Johnson Market a culinary landmark, where legendary kebab houses, iconic rolls and beloved local eateries reflect generations of migration and cultural exchange.More than a heritage walk, this is a journey through the people, faiths and traditions that shaped one of Bengaluru's most distinctive neighbourhoods—revealing a side of the city that few have the opportunity to experience.

From ancient temples and ashrams to grand old churches and the revered Gurudwara every corner has a tale to tell. Learn how this area grew into a melting pot of traditions giving rise to its bustling markets serene kalyani (temple tank) and vibrant festivals including the much-anticipated annual “Poo Palakki” a floral chariot procession that brings the streets alive with color and devotion.  As we navigate through the lively bazaars you’ll catch glimpses of charming heritage homes—relics from a bygone era—standing as silent witnesses to the evolution of this neighborhood. We’ll conclude our journey with a taste of authentic South Indian snacks and refreshing beverages giving you a perfect blend of history culture and flavors to take home.  Come step back in time with us and rediscover Ulsoor like never before!

name: Cottonpete heritage walk.
description: Our fourth journey through the historic quarters of Kempe Gowda’s Pettah unfolds under a theme as timeless as it is universal—the search for Faith. Few places in Bengaluru bear witness to such layered expressions of belief, practice, and community as this old quarter, where stones, shrines, and stories alike speak of lives entwined with devotion.We begin in the western precincts of Pettah, which has one of the city’s most significant Sufi dargahs. For well over two centuries this shrine has stood not merely as a site of veneration but as a living symbol of spiritual devotion and communal harmony. Here, the life of the saint and the mystical traditions of Sufism unfold before us, reminding visitors of how such spaces once bridged communities across faiths, drawing pilgrims, merchants, and seekers into a shared spiritual geography.From the domain of sacred devotion we turn toward the realm of healing. In the narrow lanes nearby still operate age-old Ayurvedic massage centers, famed above all for their bone-setting traditions. Local memory recalls how the Maharajas of Mysore themselves entrusted these practitioners, as did the pahalwans of the akhadas—wrestling arenas that once gave Pettah its distinctive physical culture. In these practices of cure and discipline, body and faith intertwined, shaping a distinctly urban form of resilience and well-being.Our steps then carry us to venerable temples associated with saints whose teachings left a lasting imprint on the identity of this quarter. Within their carved stones and sanctums endures a layered continuity—of memory, worship, and the rhythm of everyday devotion. Time permitting, the trail may extend toward a garadi mane (wrestling house) or an old heritage lodge, each bearing traces of the social fabric of an earlier Bengaluru, when physical culture and communal gathering defined neighborhood life.The walk also includes a South Indian breakfast in heritage restaurant, where history, faith, and community meet in lived experience.This walk is guided by an architect whose professional eye discerns the city’s built heritage, and whose personal practice of Sufism and passion for food lend the journey both intimacy and delight. His explorations carry him to parts of Bengaluru often absent from tourist maps, offering participants not simply a tour, but an immersion into the city’s layered heart.

name: Kalighat Painting Workshop
description: KALIGHAT PAINTINGS – WHERE TRADITION MEETS MODERNITYBengal is renowned for its rich cultural heritage and diverse artistic traditions, including music, literature, dance, and visual arts. In this workshop, we will explore one of Bengal's most fascinating and thought-provoking art forms—Kalighat Paintings.Bold, expressive & vibrant, Kalighat paintings beautifully bring together a variety of themes, ranging from Hindu mythology and spirituality to secular life and social commentary.Originating in 19th-century Kolkata during the colonial period, this distinctive art form developed around the Kalighat Temple, dedicated to Goddess Kali. The paintings were traditionally created on patas (cloth or paper scrolls) by artists known as Patuas. Located near the banks of the Hooghly River and the popular Kalighat Temple, the area attracted pilgrims, locals, and foreign visitors, creating a thriving audience for these unique artworks.However, with the growing popularity of printed reproductions in the early 20th century, traditional handmade Kalighat paintings gradually declined.The legacy of this expressive art form was later reinterpreted and celebrated by renowned Indian artist Jamini Roy, who drew inspiration from Bengal's folk traditions and brought a distinctive modern interpretation to traditional Indian art.What will you learn?Learn about the history and evolution of Kalighat PaintingsExplore the life and artistic journey of Jamini RoyUnderstand the distinctive themes, styles, and visual language of this art formDiscover how traditional Indian folk art influenced modern artistic expressionCreate your very own Kalighat-inspired paintingThis will be a wonderful opportunity to experience Indian art and culture through storytelling, learning, and hands-on creativity!Note:All art materials required for the workshop will be provided by the host.What will you take home?A Detailed Hands-On Workshop WorkbookKnowledge & History of Kalighat art & cultureYour very own completed artwork created during the workshopWhat do you need to bring?A water bottle to keep yourself hydrated.All workshop materials will be provided. name: Avenue Road (Pete) heritage walk.
description: Step into Bengaluru’s oldest quarter and travel almost 500 years into the past to the original Pete—a world of fortified walls, bustling bazaars, temples, mosques, merchants, and craftsmen.This is where the city’s story begins, from one end of Avenue Road to the other. Meet Kempe Gowda I, the visionary chieftain who founded Bengaluru, and discover why he chose this unlikely corner of the Deccan. What drew him here, and what strange signs, according to legend, foretold the birth of the city?Next comes one of Bengaluru’s most haunting tales: the legend of the Southern Gate of the Pete, involving a pregnant woman, a sacrifice, and the building of the city’s earliest fortifications.Kempe Gowda’s settlement, however, was never destined to remain a small fortified town. Within a century, Bengaluru’s strategic location and growing wealth made it a coveted prize for the Bijapur Sultanate, the Marathas, and eventually the Mughals, before the city passed into the hands of the Mysore kingdom and, after the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, the British.What made Bengaluru so valuable? What did the original Bangalore Fort look like? And how did this fortified town of bazaars and bastions evolve into the sprawling metropolis we know today?Beyond the monuments, we discover the people who made the Pete thrive—merchants, craftsmen, saints, philanthropists, and religious communities whose stories still linger in its streets. Along the way, you will discover historic temples, the KR Market, Sufi shrines, forgotten landmarks, and some of Bengaluru’s oldest neighbourhoods.No journey through the Pete is complete without food, so we will finish with delicious local snacks at an iconic old eatery tucked just off the road.Come discover the Bengaluru that came before the metropolis. Walk its oldest streets, uncover its forgotten stories, and see the city through an entirely new lens.

description: Goonj ka GharThursday, 26th November, 7.30 p.m. - 8.20 p.m.Language: Hindi (with subtitles in English)About the PerformanceGoonj ka Ghar is a physical theatre performance that combines movement, minimal set design, and fragmented storytelling to explore themes of identity, power, and marginalisation. Initially inspired by three seminal short stories, Tirichh by Uday Prakash, Toba Tek Singh by Saadat Hasan Manto, and Uljhan by Vijaydan Detha, which are woven into a single theatrical narrative that interrogates unresolved questions of identity, belonging and justice in today’s world.Set against the backdrop of a society grappling with citizenship, identity and social justice, the performance raises urgent questions: What makes a person a citizen? What do we call home when borders both physical and psychological remain in flux? Who is considered sane, worthy, beautiful, or legitimate? Why does society continue to value women who appear silent and submissive? Each segment reflects marginalisation through a distinct lens — surreal satire on madness and displacement, dark allegory on invisibility and class, and an introspective exploration of gender, self-worth and systemic injustice.CastACT IMaya: NaginaHusband and Bhola: AslamACT IICricketer: SaddamFriend and Officer: ShahidMadam Officer: NaginaACT IIIOora: IsmailCrewDirection: Nagina, Naghma and JasmineSound and Light: Jasmine and NaghmaSet Design: Nagina, Jasmine and NaghmaStage Crew: Shahid, Ismail and AabshaarMovement Direction, Rehearsal and Production Support: AabshaarProduction Coordinator: Sanyukta and ShoaibAbout the ArtistsSanyukta SahaSanyukta Saha is a theatre pedagogue, facilitator and community arts leader, and the Founder and Executive Director of Aagaaz Theatre Trust, a community-rooted arts organisation in New Delhi. Her work focuses on participatory arts-based learning processes with children, adolescents, youth and women, using theatre, dialogue and reflection to explore questions of identity, citizenship, gender, well-being and belonging.Sanyukta holds an MA in Theatre and Development Studies from the University of Leeds, UK, and a BA in English Literature from the University of Delhi. She has taught and facilitated learning processes at Ashoka University and the University of Delhi, and has also been involved in mentoring through the Bargad Theatre Fellowship.She has over 17 years of experience working across theatre, education and community-based practice. Before founding Aagaaz Theatre Trust in 2015, she worked as Arts Education Programme Coordinator with the Aga Khan Foundation, where she designed and implemented arts-integrated education programmes in the neighbourhood government school in Basti Hazrat Nizamuddin and early childhood centres. She has also worked as a theatre facilitator and community practitioner with Pandies' Theatre and through her independent practice.At Aagaaz, Sanyukta leads the organisation's strategy and overall development, while continuing to facilitate, mentor and develop participatory creative processes with young people and communities.AslamAslam has been performing with the Repertory since 2015. As an actor and facilitator, he has participated in theatre festivals, schools, public venues, open spaces, and national events. He facilitates drama- and arts-based learning spaces for adolescent boys in Nizamuddin Basti. He has recently directed a work in progress play called Chaukidar. Aslam is also a professional rugby player, coach, and referee with Delhi Wolves.Naghma Naghma is one of the younger powerhouses in the group. name: How Not to Build a Theatre Institution
description: How Not to Build a Theatre InstitutionA Conversation with Abhishek Mudgal, Sanyukta Saha and Abhishek Majumdar, moderated by Priyanka Varma Friday, 27th November, 5.00 p.m. - 6.30 p.m.About the ConversationArtists establish and lead theatre institutions (which include long-standing initiatives) for different reasons — to practice, teach, present, advocate or support the art form, for instance.But such undertakings, especially if they function independently of secure government or corporate largesse, can falter or fail. The poverty of infrastructure and support for the theatre are among the external factors that are adduced for the precariousness of artist-led institutions. Internal factors are rarely cited. What if the institution is over-reliant on personal equations and goodwill for its sustenance? Or if its ownership is narrowly concentrated in one or two charismatic personalities? Or if it is too obsessed with legacy concerns to avert obsolescence in a swiftly changing environment?This session will investigate what might lie inside any theatre institution that could threaten its stability and hamper its growth. Reflecting on their personal experience of founding and running institutions, three theatre artists will tell us about what worked or did not work about the choices they made. Were discontents allowed to simmer, tensions swept under the carpet or challenges left unaddressed? In hindsight, do they regret any missteps or wish they had done some things differently?About the Participants Sanyukta SahaSanyukta Saha is a theatre pedagogue, facilitator and community arts leader, and the Founder and Executive Director of Aagaaz Theatre Trust, a community-rooted arts organisation in New Delhi. She has also worked as a theatre facilitator and community practitioner with Pandies' Theatre and through her independent practice.At Aagaaz, Sanyukta leads the organisation's strategy and overall development, while continuing to facilitate, mentor and develop participatory creative processes with young people and communities.﻿Abhishek MajumdarAbhishek Majumdar is a writer and director, working across theatre, novels, essays, film and opera. name: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre
description: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre A Conversation with Sharanya Ramprakash, Laya N Kumar and Parshathy J Nath, moderated by Lakshmana KP Saturday, 28th November, 4.30 p.m. - 6.00 p.m.About the ConversationThe traditions with which contemporary urban Indian theatre artists can engage are immense, embracing mythologies, folk tales and performances, art and craft objects and practices, festivals and rituals, cuisine, inherited knowledge and skills, and much else besides. At the same time, the distinction between the traditional and the modern is not clearcut. Modern theatre in India has a history that stretches back for over two centuries — long enough to develop its own traditions. Dance forms now regarded as ‘classical’ acquired modern practices of teaching, performance and patronage in the last century.The theatre artists in this session will speak about their idea of tradition and how they have interacted with it in the plays they have written, directed or performed. They will also be invited to discuss ethical and political questions that come to the fore when tradition is brought into contemporary theatre work. Has their work been sensitive to the claim that borrowing from inherited forms of expression can constitute a form of cultural theft or disrespects localised and context-specific creation of value and meaning? How would they negotiate with traditions that have been invented in response to market demands or political pressures? Has their work reconciled with, or has it offered a critical perspective on the feudalism, casteism and gender discrimination embedded in many traditional performances and stories?About the ParticipantsSharanya Ramprakash Sharanya Ramprakash is a Bengaluru-based theatre-maker. She places her work at the intersection of gender, tradition and language. She writes, acts, directs and collaborates with a range of forms, communities and theatre-makers across local, national and international locations. Her work is research-based, collaborative and exploratory. She is a member of the Lincoln Centre Director’s Lab, New York. She is also a recipient of the Shankar Nag Theatre Award 2022.Parshathy J NathParshathy J Nath is a theatre artist based in Bengaluru. Over the last ten years, she has worked with some of the best-known theatre directors in south India, including Prasanna Ramaswamy, Rajiv Krishnan, Vinay Kumar, Nimmy Raphel, Sharanya Ramprakash, Aruna Ganesh Ram, Koumarane Valavane and Sanjeeva Suvarna. She has trained at Adishakti Laboratory for Theatre Art Research, Ninasam and Natanakairali. In 2025, she received a production grant from the India Foundation for Arts, with which she created a solo performance piece called Shoorpanakha: A Search. name: Dramatherapy
description: DramatherapyExperience Sharing by Vardhan DeshpandeSaturday, 28th November, 3.00 p.m. - 4.00 p.m.About the SessionIn this session, Vardhan Deshpande reflects on his journey with Dramatherapy and its possibilities as a practice of healing, expression and transformation.Over the past two-and-a-half years, he has been working with children at risk through Dramatherapy sessions, alongside six months of work with specially-abled children. This journey has involved much more than conducting sessions — it has been a continuous process of observing, designing, planning, facilitating, implementing, documenting and reflecting. Each group and every individual encounter has shaped his understanding of how theatre, play, imagination, embodiment, storytelling and creative expression can create spaces for children to explore themselves, connect with others and experience agency.The session will share key experiences from this practice: the challenges encountered, the learning that emerged, the questions that continue to remain, and the ways in which reflection has influenced subsequent interventions. It will also look towards the future — considering how Dramatherapy and Applied Theatre can evolve in working with children and communities, and the ethical, creative and contextual sensitivities that such practice demands.About the SpeakerVardhan DeshpandeVardhan Deshpande works as a theatre facilitator in schools and colleges. He also works as a storyteller-actor-director for children's plays and conducts theatre workshops for children and adults. Since March 2024, he has also worked as a theatre facilitator for juveniles in the Child Welfare Committee, Pune, with the NGO - 'Foundation for Child Protection - Muskaan'. This committee acts as a crucial safety net for vulnerable children, providing them with the care, protection and support they need to thrive. name: unLecture x Gully Labs Bangalore
description: Five very different conversations. One very curious city.Bangalore, we're here!! And we're bringing you five sessions that go from the psychology of power to the politics of citizenship, from economics that turns everything you thought you knew on its head to robots dreaming of Mars, and poetry that asks what it means to keep feeling things in a world that can be a little too much.We're revisiting one of psychology's most famous experiments, questioning who gets to belong in a democracy, finding out why good intentions can make terrible policies, meeting the robots that could one day assist astronauts, and spending an evening with poetry, power, and pleasure.Basically, a little psychology, a little politics, a little science, and a lot of things to think about long after you leave.31st October: The Stanford Prison Experiment: Who Gave You That Power?Ganga M NairThe experiment lasted six days. The legend got a life sentence. We all know the story of ordinary people given power and what supposedly happened next. But what does the experiment actually tell us about human behaviour? And how does power show up in our group chats, relationships, family lunches, and Monday meetings? Through behavioural psychology, neuroscience, and a few experiments on ourselves, we'll unpack the power dynamics hiding in plain sight.1st November: SIR and the Crisis of Documentary CitizenshipAdil HossainWhat does it mean to belong to a country, and who gets to decide? Looking at the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls through the lens of documentary citizenship, political anthropologist Adil Hossain examines how documents, identity, religion, and ideas of belonging shape who gets recognised as a citizen — and who risks being excluded.14th November: The Counter-Intuitive Economist: Stories About Why Good Intentions Make Bad PolicyAnupam ManurIs a cotton tote really better for the planet than a plastic bag? Are higher prices during a disaster always a bad thing? And why do attempts to cut out middlemen so often fail? Professor Anupam Manur takes us through the economic ideas hiding behind everyday assumptions, using stories that challenge what we think we know. No equations, no jargon, just a few surprises about how the world works.22nd November: VLA Rovers: From Assistive Household Companions to Mars ExplorationPradipta BoseWhat if a robot could understand what you say, see the world around it, and figure out what to do next? From assistive technologies that translate eye movements into actions to intelligent rovers designed for the challenges of space, Prof. Pradipta Bose explores how vision-language-action models are changing the way humans and robots work together — on Earth and potentially on Mars.28th November: Zulmaton ke Daur Mein: An Evening of Poetry, Power, and PleasureNeha MishraWhat is the point of poetry in a world that often seems determined to do without it? From Plato's attempts to banish poetry from his Republic to contemporary attempts to regulate art and literature, this session explores why poetry continues to matter. Through a selection of poems, we'll think about emotion, pleasure, politics, and how reading might help us find our way through the overwhelming despair of our times.Five sessions, five different rabbit holes, and hopefully a whole lot of new questions.Bangalore, come curious. Leave with something to think about.

name: GFT: November Edition in Bangalore
description: Grounds for Thought: Bangalore, November 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three evenings. Three very different conversations. Grounds for Thought brings researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into rooms full of curious people, where the conversation goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This November in Bangalore runs from constitutional literacy to the history of economic ideas, closing with a reframing of how India's princely states shaped its founding.15th November: Anjor BhaskarDemocracy is declining around the world, Why don't young people care?Democracy doesn't die when constitutions fail — it dies when citizens stop practising democratic values. Anjor Bhaskar, faculty at Azim Premji University and founder of Dialogues on Democracy and Development, has worked with over 30,000 participants across India on what he calls constitutional literacy: translating values like liberty, equality, and fraternity into everyday practice. This session asks why so many young people know more about celebrities than the Constitution, why misinformation outruns truth so easily, and why constitutional morality may be the most important skill nobody is teaching.21st November: Alex M. ThomasFantastic Economic Theories and Where to Find Them Are wages and interest rates "fantastic" in the sense of excellent — or in the sense of hard to believe? Alex M. Thomas, Associate Professor of Economics at Azim Premji University and author of the widely used textbook Macroeconomics: An Introduction, takes this question through the history of economic ideas: does raising the minimum wage really raise unemployment? Does the rate of interest actually capture how people value the present over the future? An interactive session that moves from classical political economy to a sharper way of thinking about economic policy — and who it's really for.28th November: Shruti ViswanathanPrincely States and Constitutionalism: Uncovering the Many Imaginations of People, Power and Politics India's founding is usually told as a story with two actors — British India, and from 1946, the Constituent Assembly. Shruti Viswanathan, founder of The Equals Project and a graduate of NLSIU Bangalore and the Fletcher School at Tufts, argues that leaves out a third: the roughly 565 princely states governing a third of the subcontinent's population, usually mentioned only at the moment of their accession, as a problem to be solved rather than as sites of constitutional thought in their own right. This session reframes their integration as a provocation — revealing that the "Idea of India" was never a single, inevitable outcome, but a fiercely contested space with constitutional activity of its own, often well before 1947.

name: The Hidden Framework with Krupalini Swamy
description: Before you had words, you were handed a framework: for who to be, what to want, how to react.From caregivers and schooling to social structures and cultural expectation, we inherit belief systems long before we can question them. They become the invisible architecture behind our choices. The Hidden Framework is an in-person workshop that makes that architecture visible, so it stops running you unseen.Is this for you? If you snap, shrink or over-give on cue and can't quite explain why, if you chase goals measured against a yardstick you were handed, or if the same arguments keep repeating with different people, this session is for you.How the session works: a guided, structured self-inquiry. Not therapy, not a lecture. Three movements: See it forming (how a framework gets built through caregivers, schooling, social structures and culture). See who it belongs to (separate the rules you were given from the ones you would actually choose). See what's possible (not a fix, a choice made with your eyes open).Your facilitator: Krupalini Swamy is an emotional intelligence specialist, TEDx speaker and UNESCO Kindness Ambassador, and founder of The Tall Elephant. She facilitates rather than prescribes, guiding people to their own insight. Her work has been recognised by NITI Aayog, IIM Bangalore and the United Nations.English. Ages 18+. Doors open 3:30 PM. name: Present Tense: How You React Under Pressure
description: Three hours with a small group of strangers, built around the feeling before a conversation you've been putting off.What We'll DoMost of us already know what we want to say in a hard moment. What gets in the way is the reaction that turns up first: the tight chest, the blank mind, the version of you that says less than you meant. That reaction is a reflex, and it rarely shows itself somewhere you can look at it.In the room, we take away the things you usually lean on and watch what shows up instead. You're on your feet more than you're seated, working in pairs and small groups. Nothing is scripted, nobody performs for an audience, and you can pass on anything without giving a reason. Then you try something different, and try it again.About Present TensePresent Tense has run twice in Bengaluru. Each time, people noticed their bodies react before they could name what they were feeling, and more than one found it easier to accept applause for a failure than for something they'd done well. None of that is a promise about what happens to you. It's what has happened in the rooms so far.presenttense.club/Perfect ForAnyone who knows the feeling before something that matters and would rather understand it than push through it. People who've come so far include founders, product managers, doctors, architects, lawyers and engineers. What they had in common was the feeling, not the job. Come alone. Most people do.Meet Your HostsYash and Praveen have run rooms together for four years, around 250 sessions with over two thousand people, most of them first-timers. Yash spends his week with founders and business owners, and is good at the part nobody notices: spotting the person who's gone quiet. Praveen designs the sessions and runs a company, which means the conversations this afternoon is built around are ones he puts off too.

name: Mehfil Mushaiira: Bangalore
description: Mehfil Mushaiira // an evening of Urdu poetry, ghazals and music, with one twist: by the end of it, the audience gets to be the poet.The best mehfils were never on posters; you heard about them from someone who’d been. So if you’ve found your way here, either someone thinks you belong in the room, or you went digging. Both count :))// Somewhere along the way, most of us filed ourselves under “not the creative type.” The poems stayed in our heads, the sketchbooks stayed in a drawer, and we became professional listeners. This evening is here to mess with that a little.At the door, you get an Urdu word. It’s yours for the night, no returns. We sit with it first, until it stops being a dictionary entry and starts sounding like someone you know. Then the mehfil takes over: live shayari, ghazals and music, a crash course in Mehfil ke Adaab (yes, there’s a right way to say “wah”), and blank canvases for when the music gets to you. Somewhere in all of it, your word starts writing back. In the last half hour, the mic turns around. Read, sing, recite, or just send a loud “wah wah” from your seat. Nobody gets graded. Daad is compulsory.You don’t have to be an artist to experience the artist’s delight.🕯️ Sunday, 29 November · 7:00 pm to 10:00 pm📍 Sabha Blr, BangaloreCome alone, or drag along the friend who swears they “aren’t creative.” Especially that one.A Mehfil Eve by Kaunversations <3

name: The Knowledge Continuum
description: Join us at Shoonya for a workshop with Loksutr, a Madhya Pradesh-based publishing and research-design initiative founded by Achyut Siddu and Apoorva Mishra. Working closely with indigenous communities and traditional artists, Loksutr transforms oral histories, collective memory and traditional knowledge systems into richly illustrated visual narratives, books and other creative formats.The Knowledge Continuum is a hands-on, process-driven workshop by Loksutr that invites participants to explore the stories, histories and knowledge systems that shape their everyday lives. Through visual documentation, creative exploration and collective learning, participants will work towards creating their own visual storylines — drawing from personal memories, lived experiences, inherited knowledge and the worlds around them.The workshop encourages participants to look closely, document what often goes unrecorded, and discover ways of translating their experiences and knowledge into visual narratives. It is an opportunity to engage with storytelling as a living, evolving process — one that connects the past, present and future.Loksutr works at the intersection of indigenous knowledge, visual storytelling, design and publishing. Through collaborations with knowledge keepers, community storytellers and traditional artists, they document oral traditions, myths, rituals, ecological knowledge and cultural practices, translating them into illustrated manuscripts, books, installations and contemporary visual formats.Their practice is rooted in the belief that traditional knowledge is not merely a record of the past, but a living resource that continues to shape how communities understand and engage with the world.

description: The day is done. Your mind isn't.11:40 pm. Laptop shut. Twelve tabs still open in your head.If you are good at your job and quietly worn out, this is for you. Not in crisis, not looking for therapy. You have probably tried a meditation app and dropped it within a week. You just want your evenings back without stepping off the career track.The Live Reset Room is a 90-minute, phones-off session where you learn a 10-minute daily reset for an overloaded mind, one you can start the same night:- 5 minutes of slow breathing, out longer than in, no counting- 5 short written lines using the 5R method: Recognize, Release, Reframe, Resolve, ReflectWHAT HAPPENS IN THE ROOM- Phones go into a basket at the door- Guided slow breathing, and a few minutes of shared silence- The 5R writing method, on paper, together- A short, honest look at what this practice can and cannot do- You leave knowing exactly how to repeat it at home in ten minutesWHAT YOU TAKE HOME- A Karungali pendant: something to hold that cues you to slow down. The 5R method was the most useful part." - Rahul, Founder, High on Shifthttps://www.instagram.com/p/DfsI15fl1Pu/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&avpt=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==ABOUT THE PRACTICE AND THE JOURNALThe practice comes from Ambitious & Grounded, GoDivinely's 90-day journal. It is a research-backed method: slow breathing with a longer out-breath, naming a feeling in a word, and writing one specific next step are each studied techniques, and every study is listed in the journal's Evidence Notes, along with its limits. The method has been reviewed by a practising psychologist. It was tested in the first Live Reset Room before it went into the book. You do not need the journal to attend: the session teaches the whole practice. The practice started with his own bad year: doing well on paper, quietly running on empty, and a mind that had forgotten how to slow down.
